the_story: Indian farmers are struggling to plant winter crops because of dwindling water supplies caused by a weak monsoon.
A farmer named Amarsingh Gushinge's village faces a significant rainfall deficit, which is changing crop planting decisions.
Food inflation could get worse as key staples see rising prices, adding heavy economic strain to everyday households.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) [India's central bank that controls money supply and interest rates] may respond with interest rate hikes to fight these rising price pressures.
analysis.what_happened: Indian farmers are facing major hurdles in planting winter crops because a weak monsoon left water reserves dangerously low. This shortage of water for farming is driving up key staple food prices, which in turn is pushing up overall food inflation and making household budgets much tighter.
analysis.analogy: It is like a dry summer drying up a vegetable garden, forcing you to pay much more at the local sabzi [vegetable] market while also having to pay extra just to borrow money.
why_it_matters_india: Weak monsoon and low water supplies reduce winter crop planting by farmers
Less food production leads to scarcer supplies and rising prices at grocery stores
Overall retail inflation prints higher as food costs surge across households
The RBI is pressured to raise or maintain high interest rates to cool down inflation, making loans costlier

impacts.rationale: Rising staple food prices due to poor crop planting push up overall inflation, which is bad for everyday household purchasing power.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Expectations that the RBI might hike interest rates to fight inflation push bond yields up, which generally means costlier borrowing for everyone.
If the RBI raises interest rates to combat inflation, home, car, and personal loans become more expensive — bad for borrowers.

events.headline: India’s emissions growth slows as renewable energy begins replacing coal, UNEP report finds

items.title: India’s emissions growth slows as renewable energy begins replacing coal, UNEP report finds
items.summary: The upward trend of greenhouse gas emissions in India showed a significant change in 2025. The trend, which was indicating a longer period of rapid growth, has pivoted from this path and is now showing a slight decline in India’s emissions. This has been reported in the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) new report Emissions […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

The upward trend of greenhouse gas emissions in India showed a significant change in 2025. The trend, which was indicating a longer period of rapid growth, has pivoted from this path and is now showing a slight decline in India’s emissions. This has been reported in the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) new report Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, released on October 21.

The report finds that the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) and the International Energy Agency (IEA) indicate a slight decline in India’s emissions, while the Energy Institute estimates a marginal increase. However, all three indicate a departure from the country’s earlier pattern of rapid emissions growth, partly because of weather effects and structural shifts towards renewable energy.

“The data this year is very encouraging,” said Minal Pathak, a researcher at Ahmedabad University and a lead author of the UNEP report’s chapter on global emissions trends, in a written response to Mongabay-India.

She said the change was partly attributable to weather effects and structural shifts towards renewable energy, as highlighted in Chapter 2 of the report.

India remains the world’s third-largest greenhouse gas emitter after China and the United States. Its emissions reached approximately 4.5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in 2025, excluding land use and forestry. However, its per capita emissions of 3.1 tonnes were less than half the global average of 6.4 tonnes.

A separate analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), published by Carbon Brief, estimated that India’s CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and cement increased by just 0.7% in 2025, the slowest growth since 2001, excluding the pandemic year of 2020.

The CREA estimate covers fossil-fuel and cement CO₂ emissions, whereas UNEP considers a broader range of greenhouse gases and emissions sources. The figures are therefore not directly comparable.

India’s renewable electricity generation increased by approximately 98 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025, according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026.

Solar generation increased by 53 TWh, or 37%, while wind added 22 TWh and hydropower approximately 21 TWh. During the same period, electricity demand increased by 49 TWh, or 2.4%, compared with 6.2% growth in 2024.

Meanwhile, coal-fired electricity generation declined by 44 TWh, or 2.9%. Coal’s share of electricity generation fell from approximately 75% in 2024 to 71% in 2025.

Vaibhav Chaturvedi, a researcher at the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) and a contributing author of Chapter 4 of the UNEP report, said the figures indicate a potentially important change.

“The 2025 figures suggest that renewables are beginning to displace coal rather than simply meet new demand. But this is an emerging shift, and adding clean energy capacity alone will not sustain it unless the power sector can store, transmit and use clean electricity when and where it is needed,” he said in a written response to Mongabay-India.

For the first time, solar overtook hydropower to become India’s largest individual source of clean electricity. Solar supplied approximately 9.4% of India’s electricity in 2025, while solar and wind together contributed around 14%.

All clean sources, including renewables and nuclear energy, accounted for approximately 27% of total electricity generation, compared with around 22% in 2024.

Despite this expansion, coal remained India’s dominant electricity source. According to Ember, coal generation was still 46% higher in 2025 than in 2015.

The reduction in coal generation also affected emissions. Ember estimates that electricity-sector greenhouse gas emissions declined by 2.9%, from 1,437 million tonnes of CO₂e in 2024 to 1,395 million tonnes in 2025.

Favourable weather conditions also influenced India’s emissions trend.

According to the India Meteorological Department’s (IMD) Statement on the Climate of India during 2025, India’s average temperature was 0.28°C above the 1991–2020 average, compared with an anomaly of 0.65°C in 2024, the warmest year on record.

Although 2025 was still India’s eighth warmest year since 1901, the relatively milder summer reduced electricity demand for cooling.

Ember estimates that lower cooling demand reduced electricity consumption by approximately 32 TWh compared with what would otherwise have been expected.

India also received approximately 1,274 millimetres of rainfall, equivalent to 110% of its long-period average. Southwest monsoon rainfall reached 108% of normal, supporting hydropower generation.

“India’s emissions growth slowed sharply in 2025, and two things explain much of it: a helpful turn in the weather, and the steady rise of clean energy,” Chaturvedi said.

“Such favourable conditions may not recur, and the benefit cannot be regarded as a long-term trend,” he cautioned.

A CREA assessment attributed 44% of the reversal in coal- and gas-fired electricity generation growth, compared with the 2019–2024 trend, to increased clean electricity generation. Another 36% was attributed to reduced cooling demand and 20% to a longer-term slowdown in electricity demand growth unrelated to weather.

These percentages describe the reversal relative to the earlier power-demand trend, not shares of India’s total emissions reductions.

Pathak cautioned against drawing direct conclusions about causes from emissions figures alone.

“We look at data on fuels and emissions, so it is difficult to infer the reason directly from emissions data,” she said.

While electricity-sector emissions declined, India’s steel and cement production continued expanding.

According to CREA’s analysis, steel production increased by approximately 8% in 2025, while cement production grew by around 10%. Together, these industries accounted for approximately 21% of India’s CO₂ emissions from fossil fue

analysis.tldr: A slowdown in India's greenhouse gas emissions and a rise in renewable energy mean cleaner air and a structural shift away from coal power, though coal remains dominant.
the_story: The UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026, released on October 21, reported that India's greenhouse gas emissions showed a significant change in 2025, pivoting from rapid growth to a slight decline or marginal increase depending on the tracking agency.

India's total emissions reached approximately 4.5 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in 2025, keeping it the world's third-largest emitter behind China and the US, with per capita emissions of 3.1 tonnes.
A separate analysis by CREA estimated that fossil-fuel and cement CO₂ emissions grew by just 0.7% in 2025, the slowest growth since 2001 outside of 2020.
Renewable electricity generation grew by about 98 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025, with solar up 53 TWh (37%), wind up 22 TWh, and hydropower up 21 TWh.

Coal-fired electricity generation fell by 44 TWh (2.9%), dropping coal's share of electricity generation from about 75% in 2024 to 71% in 2025 as renewables began replacing coal rather than just meeting new demand.
analysis.what_happened: India's greenhouse gas emissions growth slowed sharply and dipped in 2025. This was driven by two main factors: a structural shift where renewable energy sources like solar and wind began replacing coal power, and milder weather conditions that reduced the electricity needed for cooling.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household whose monthly electricity bill finally drops because they installed solar panels on the roof and had a cooler summer, meaning they rely less on burning expensive, dirty fuel.
why_it_matters_india: Renewable energy expansion increases clean electricity generation -> Solar overtakes hydropower as the largest individual source of clean electricity, supplying about 9.4% of India's electricity in 2025.
Coal generation declines -> Coal-fired electricity generation drops by 2.9%, reducing electricity-sector greenhouse gas emissions to 1,395 million tonnes of CO₂e.
Milder weather reduces energy demand -> Average temperatures were closer to normal and monsoon rainfall reached 110% of the long-period average, lowering cooling demand and boosting hydropower.
Industrial production expands -> Steel production grows by 8% and cement by 10%, showing that heavy industries continue to grow even as the power sector cuts emissions.

impacts.target: Renewable energy and clean tech sector stocks
impacts.rationale: Stronger deployment of solar and wind power creates a tailwind for companies building and operating clean energy infrastructure, which is generally positive for long-term sustainable growth.

impacts.target: Traditional coal mining and thermal power companies
impacts.rationale: A structural shift where renewables begin replacing coal means slower long-term demand growth for thermal power generators, posing challenges for traditional energy businesses.

watch_next: Whether power sector storage and transmission can keep up with rising clean energy capacity
Future weather patterns and summer cooling demands
analysis.caveats: Experts caution that favorable weather conditions may not recur and adding clean energy alone will not sustain emission reductions without better storage and transmission.

events.headline: India’s external constraints haven't disappeared—they are shapeshifting

items.title: India’s external constraints haven't disappeared—they are shapeshifting
items.summary: A smaller current account deficit is welcome, but costly global capital and financial flows that reshape importer and exporter behaviour can turn a small financing gap into outsized currency pressure. These are the external pressures policymakers must manage.

events.article_text:
A small current account deficit may not offer immunity against rupee stress. India’s external constraints are changing. Policy will need to adapt.

The current account deficit is the central gauge of external vulnerability. It measures the economy’s net external financing requirement, which must be met by foreign capital inflows. When those inflows fall short, the adjustment ultimately falls on foreign exchange reserves, domestic asset prices or the currency.

On that basis, India appears substantially more insulated than it was 10 years ago. Its trend current account deficit has fallen below 1% of gross domestic product (GDP) from more than 4% a little over a decade ago. Even with oil around $100 a barrel, we expect the deficit to remain around 1% in 2026-27. Yet the rupee is under pressure.

First, global financing conditions have changed. Structurally higher interest rates and enormous demand for risk capital from global technology firms have made capital scarcer and costlier for emerging markets.

Returns on US corporate assets are rising much faster than those in India and broader Asia. Meanwhile, the 10-year US government debt offers a risk-free yield of 5%, versus 1% five or six years ago. A fully-hedged investment in India’s 10-year sovereign debt yields less than 4% today.

These factors give global investors little incentive to expand their emerging-market portfolios. Under such tight global financial conditions, India’s financially feasible trend current account deficit may be little more than 0.5% of GDP today, making historical benchmarks of 2.5% to 3% irrelevant.

Second, the current account’s composition matters, as net external financing and gross forex needs are not the same thing. The improvement in India’s current account deficit has been lopsided, driven largely by a growing services surplus and remittance inflows. Meanwhile, the core goods trade deficit, excluding oil and gold imports, has widened, by about 2% of GDP relative to its average over the past decade.

India’s high growth, in other words, has not come without greater external imbalance in goods trade. This is also visible in the import-to-GDP ratio, which has risen to about 25% from 20% five or six years ago. Growth, thus, continues to generate substantial gross demand for foreign currency even when the net current-account balance looks benign.

This is particularly true when growth is investment-led, given the economy’s reliance on imported capital goods, energy and intermediate inputs, demand for which is relatively insensitive to price in the short run.

Third, the rupee’s behaviour has changed. Gross financial-account flows are now almost as large as gross current-account flows. Alongside trade, relative asset returns, global risk appetite and portfolio allocations shape the rupee. Financial signals arrive much faster than trade flows, allowing expectations to shift rapidly.

That matters because expectations affect the behaviour of firms that actually buy and sell foreign currency. The prolonged weakness in financial flows, particularly equity, has entrenched expectations of rupee depreciation amid adverse global factors.

Importers and exporters then have asymmetric incentives. Importers expecting further depreciation may bring forward forex purchases, increase hedge ratios or lengthen hedge tenors. Exporters have the opposite incentive: converting forex receipts or locking in forward rates becomes less attractive. Their underlying imports and exports need not change for the balance of gross forex demand and supply to change.

Data provides evidence consistent with this behaviour. The Clearing Corporation of India’s client data shows aggregate importer hedge ratios rising since late 2024, especially around episodes when global shocks changed the expected path of the rupee. The weighted-average maturity of importer hedges has also risen. Meanwhile, forward forex purchases have increasingly exceeded forward sales.

This separates net external financing needs from gross forex-market pressure. A small current account deficit measures India’s net financing needs, not importers’ immediate forex demand or exporters’ willingness to supply dollars. So, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may need to bridge a timing mismatch far larger than the overall balance-of-payments deficit suggests. Its combined spot and forward interventions have exceeded the deficit in recent quarters.

So, though the current account is relevant, assessing its composition, the global cost and availability of capital, and how financial flows and expectations interact with commercial forex flows are crucial.

RBI need not aggressively resist rupee depreciation. Persistent global shocks may warrant greater exchange-rate adjustment after all. Intervention may work better by creating a perception of two-way risk than by defending predictable levels: once markets can anticipate RBI’s response, its deterrent effect weakens. Unequivocally hawkish monetary policy communication can reinforce this approach.

India’s external vulnerability has not disappeared; it has changed form. A smaller current account deficit is welcome, but costly global capital and financial flows that reshape importer and exporter behaviour can turn a small financing gap into outsized currency pressure. These are the external constraints policymakers must manage.

analysis.tldr: Global capital moving out can keep the rupee under pressure, making imported items and foreign travel pricier for everyday Indians.
the_story: India's trend current account deficit (net money flowing in and out of the country) has dropped below 1% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP, total value of goods and services produced), down from over 4% a decade ago.
Higher US interest rates (the cost of borrowing money) and soaring returns on US tech and corporate assets make global investors less likely to put money into emerging markets like India.
India's goods trade deficit (gap between what we buy and sell abroad), excluding oil and gold, has widened by about 2% of GDP compared to its past decade average.
Importers are increasingly buying hedges (financial safety tools to protect against currency drops) and rushing to buy foreign currency early because they expect the rupee to weaken further.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI, India's central bank) has had to intervene heavily in currency markets, with spot and forward interventions exceeding the actual deficit in recent quarters.
analysis.what_happened: Even though India's net current account deficit looks small, the rupee is still under pressure. This happens because global interest rates are much higher now, making foreign investors pull money toward safer US assets, and because fast domestic economic growth creates a huge raw demand for imported goods and foreign currency.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household that earns enough to cover its monthly grocery bill (small current account deficit), but struggles because its credit card debt costs much more to service and local stores demand upfront cash immediately.
why_it_matters_india: Higher US interest rates attract global capital away from emerging markets ->
Foreign investors pull money out or slow down investments in Indian assets ->
Importers rush to buy foreign currency early while exporters hold onto dollars, creating a shortage ->
The rupee faces depreciation pressure, making imported crude oil, electronics, and overseas travel more expensive for everyone.

impacts.rationale: Tight global financial conditions and strong corporate demand for foreign currency keep downward pressure on the rupee, making imports costlier for consumers.

impacts.target: Imported goods (like electronics and crude oil)
impacts.rationale: A weaker rupee means India has to pay more rupees for the same amount of imported oil and goods, which is generally bad for household budgets.

analysis.caveats: Global capital flows and risk appetite can shift rapidly if US economic growth or Federal Reserve policies change unexpectedly.

events.article_text:

What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

After shedding 7% yesterday, crude oil prices inched up earlier today following a Wall Street Journal report about a U.S. strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island.

Brent crude traded at $105.26 per barrel at the time of writing, and West Texas Intermediate traded at $97.07 per barrel, after the WSJ cited unnamed U.S. officials as saying Iran’s Qeshm Island became a target in what they said was the latest in a series of “ limited strikes Washington has secretly carried out” over the past few weeks on Iran.

The report counters earlier media coverage about continued diplomatic efforts to end the war that has caused the most severe disruption in global oil and gas supply in history. It also goes against coverage indicating President Trump was not determined to resume strikes on Iran.

“We had a war with Iran. We won,” Trump told media on Monday, as quoted by the Wall Street Journal. “I don’t know if you even call it a war because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.”

“The report added a degree of risk premium back into the oil price. Just when markets were starting to price in a more diplomatic path, this reminder of ongoing military activity has flipped the tone,” Reuters quoted KCM Trade analyst Tim Waterer as saying earlier today.

Indeed, hopes about a diplomatic solution to the conflict drove oil prices lower at the start of the week, as traders ignored Iran statements that all seven of its conditions would need to be met in order for a peace deal to be agreed, focusing instead on the very fact of talks being held—between Iranian and Qatari officials.

Some believe the war premium is already factored into prices and any future rally would only take place if physical oil supply gets disrupted additionally. “Unless there is concrete evidence of further disruption to physical supplies or critical energy infrastructure, fresh headlines alone may struggle ‌to sustain another rally,” Phillip Nova’s Priyanka Sachdeva said, as quoted by Reuters.

the_story: Crude oil prices bounced back slightly after dropping 7% the day before.
The bounce happened because of a Wall Street Journal report about a secret U.S. strike on Iran's Qeshm Island.
Brent crude (an international benchmark for oil pricing) traded at $105.26 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate (an American oil benchmark) traded at $97.07 per barrel.
The report surprised markets that were previously hoping for a diplomatic peace deal between the U.S. and Iran.
analysis.what_happened: Crude oil prices went up because a news report reminded traders that military conflict in the Middle East is still happening. Earlier, traders thought peace talks would stop the fighting, which caused oil prices to fall. But the news of U.S. strikes on Iran brought back fear, making traders add a risk premium (extra cost added to an asset's price because of uncertainty or danger) to oil prices.
analysis.analogy: It is like a neighbourhood grocery store suddenly raising its prices because a delivery truck got delayed by a roadblock, even though the store owner hopes the road will clear up tomorrow.

Global oil prices jump up due to fear of supply disruptions ->

events.headline: BYD expands EV shipping fleet as wars upend freight costs and key trade routes

items.title: BYD expands EV shipping fleet as wars upend freight costs and key trade routes
items.summary: The ''BYD Explorer No. 1'' car carrier, loaded with new energy vehicles, is setting sail from Yantai Port in Yantai, China, on January 10, 2024.

events.article_text:
China’s BYDiBYDBYD Auto is a Chinese carmaker that became the world’s leading EV manufacturer in 2023, competing with Tesla for market share and global attention.READ MORE is building cars faster than it can export, so it’s adding more ships.

The world’s largest electric vehicle maker will expand its fleet of car-carrying cargo ships to 18 from eight by 2029, according to shipping industry reports. Each new carrier will have the capacity to carry about 9,200 cars and will be built by China Merchants Industry.

Owning its fleet could cut BYD’s cost to ship each car abroad by as much as 40% compared with renting carriers, according to one industry estimate. BYD’s increasing export capacity could help it push further into global markets, intensifying competition for automakers including Tesla and traditional U.S. brands.

“Carmakers like BYD, which invested in the sector ahead of the surge, are reaping the rewards of that long-term strategy,” Andrea De Luca, a maritime analyst at Boston-based shipping data company Veson Nautical, told Rest of World. “By owning their ships, they can save money compared with chartering at today’s elevated rates, prioritize their most important markets, enter new ones more easily, and depend less on charter market swings.”

BYD did not respond to Rest of World’s request for comment.

In 2022, BYD announced a plan worth $687 million to build its own car carriers, to fix what founder Wang Chuanfu called a shortage of shipping capacity for exports. Between January 2024 and September 2025, the company put eight car carriers into service.

Earlier this year, BYD told investors that a shortage of shipping capacity had held back its exports. In September, the company sold 180,700 cars outside China, more than double a year ago and almost 40% of its monthly total sales.

Wars in the Red Sea and around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed up freight costs and forced ships onto longer routes around conflict zones. Renting a car carrier with capacity of about 6,500 cars now costs $95,000 a day, up from $50,000 in February, according to shipping data and analytics firm Clarksons Research. Chinese owners account for only about 10% of global car carrier capacity, including ships on order, so carmakers from the country hire ships from international shipping companies, the research arm of shipbroker Clarksons said.

With BYD aiming to sell more than 2.5 million cars overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year, owning a fleet cushions against higher shipping bills and gives more control over space and routes, analysts said.

2.5 million Number of cars BYD aims to sell overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year.

“The very strong growth in Chinese exports, fueling strong Asia-Europe fronthaul demand growth, is the biggest single factor behind the increase in charter rates,” Stephen Gordon, managing director of Clarksons Research, told Rest of World. “Additionally, conflict in the Middle East has caused regional disruption and inefficiencies, which have helped to further tighten markets after a two-year period of gradual normalization.”

Most car carriers on Asia-Europe routes are sailing around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Red Sea, adding about 25% to the distance and as many as 14 days to each voyage, De Luca said. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, the spot rate for moving cars from China to the Middle East has jumped to $220 per cubic meter of cargo space from $65 in February, he said.

In China, industrywide sales of EVs and plug-in hybrids fell 12% in the first eight months of the year, after the government cut tax breaks for buyers. BYD sold 33% fewer cars at home over the same period.

Many Chinese carmakers have kept their factories busy by selling surplus cars abroad as changes to tax and subsidy incentives have cooled demand at home, George Whitcombe, a senior EV analyst at London-based battery data provider Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, told Rest of World.

Exports of China-made EVs are now rising faster than their registrations overseas, pointing to a growing stock of unsold cars, he said.

“Control over its distribution network is a strategy BYD has long pursued,” Whitcombe said. “With other Chinese automakers left without their own fleet of ships and exposed to rising shipping costs, it potentially leaves them in a less competitive position to grow their overseas presence.”

Tesla, BYD’s main U.S. rival, has relied on other companies’ carriers to export from China. Its Shanghai plant shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home in the first eight months of the year. Carmakers that charter ships are more exposed to swings in the charter market than those that own them, De Luca said.

BYD’s giant carriers are mainly a marketing exercise, Felipe Munoz, founder of research platform Car Industry Analysis, told Rest of World. Owning ships has its drawbacks and advantages, he said.

“By displaying these massive carriers, it aims to project an image of power and speed to the rest of the world,” Munoz said. “It is more a political statement against the established carmakers by telling the world that BYD is moving fast and has a lot of resources to make the most advanced EVs.”

BYD’s fleet is about control, and extending into logistics is a natural step now that it exports millions of cars amid geopolitical volatility and cost swings, Lei Xing, founder of AutoXing, a Chinese auto industry consultancy, told Rest of World. BYD ships only EVs and plug-in hybrids, which need specially configured carriers, and most of its fleet runs on liquefied natural gas as ports tighten green-fuel rules, he said.

Rival Geely began running its first car carrier in 2025, on a long-term charter from London-based shipowner Zodiac Maritime. Chery set up a venture with Wuhu Shipyard in 2023 to build car carriers for its own fleet in eastern China.

“Geely, on the other hand, will be running its own ships eventually,” Lei Xing

analysis.tldr: When global shipping gets expensive due to wars, car giants like BYD build their own ships to save money, creating intense global price competition that could eventually bring cheaper electric vehicles to Indian buyers.

events.headline: War , tariffs and China : What the US midterms mean for the Asia - Pacific - Dominican Republic Post – Caribbean News , Business , Travel & Culture

items.title: War , tariffs and China : What the US midterms mean for the Asia - Pacific - Dominican Republic Post – Caribbean News , Business , Travel & Culture

events.article_text:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.

Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.

“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”

Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.

When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages.

The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.

Public opinion in the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.

“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”

Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.

On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.

The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. Asia was again hit harder than most. Cambodia faced a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.

After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools. In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour. In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”

Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.

That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.

Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.

“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”

Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea, where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait, which separates China from Taiwan, the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.

Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.

One area where analysts do expect some change is US policy on Chinese technology.

The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China, said Okun at APAC Advisors.

These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hard

analysis.tldr: Ongoing US political shifts and trade wars will keep global energy costs high and trade unpredictable, leading to potential imported inflation for India.
the_story: Asia-Pacific governments and businesses are closely watching Tuesday's US midterm elections, hoping for changes to President Donald Trump's policies on the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran and trade tariffs.

The US-Israel war on Iran has choked off Gulf oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz since January, leaving regions like the Philippines under a national energy emergency and draining foreign reserves in poorer Asian economies.
Analysts expect little change to US foreign policy or trade tariffs from a Democrat-controlled US Congress because overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority.

The Trump administration previously imposed heavy tariffs on numerous Asian nations, and despite Supreme Court rulings, has shifted to new tariffs on 60 trading partners including China, Japan, and Southeast Asian nations.

While broader trade and war policies are unlikely to shift, analysts expect the new US Congress to pass tougher restrictions on Chinese technology, including the Remote Access Security Act and the Chip Security Act.
analysis.what_happened: Asia-Pacific nations are closely watching the US midterm elections, hoping a newly empowered Democratic-controlled Congress might force changes on the US-Israel war on Iran and heavy trade tariffs. However, experts note that structural political hurdles mean President Trump's major policies on war and trade are unlikely to change.
analysis.analogy: It is like watching a landlord fight with the neighbors over who controls the main water pipe to the building — even if the building tenants vote for a new committee, the main valve stays jammed shut.
why_it_matters_india: US and Israel's war on Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz constrained -> Gulf oil and gas flows are restricted -> Global crude oil prices remain elevated.
High global crude prices increase import costs for Asian economies -> India imports most of its oil, raising domestic fuel and transportation expenses.
Higher fuel costs feed into broader domestic price rises -> India's inflation rate goes up, reducing household purchasing power.

events.headline: Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

items.title: Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements
items.summary: Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

events.article_text:
An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955.

events.headline: Will New Laws Finally End Human Rights Abuses in Asia’s Factories?

items.title: Will New Laws Finally End Human Rights Abuses in Asia’s Factories?
items.summary: It’s clear that voluntary measures aren’t enough for ethical sourcing and supply chains.

events.article_text:
In 2000, the United Nations Global Compact was founded, and in 2007, it became the main force behind the Geneva Declaration on corporate responsibility. The idea was that companies would, voluntarily and collaboratively, work together to respect human, labor, and environmental rights in their businesses, including along complex supply chains.

The Global Compact was one of many similar initiatives, often spurred by campaigns or investigative journalism reports, that sought to end abuses in supply chains and improve sustainability. The World Benchmarking Alliance setup a corporate human rights benchmark, while the Consumer Goods Forum (CGF) launched a Human Rights Coalition. Companies including Cargill, Google, Airbus, and Coca Cola released human rights guidelines that, on paper, looked quite strict, stating clearly. For example, Microsoft declared that “suppliers must comply fully with all employment laws, share its commitment to respect all human rights… and take effective measures to remedy any adverse human rights impacts.”

Yet, more than 20 years later, the impact of these efforts are less than clear. While some companies have made progress, and shown commitment to better sourcing and monitoring of human rights along their supply chains, many have not.

“With voluntary guidelines, the key issue is the gap between commitment and real life implementation,” said Johannes Blankenbach, a researcher with the non-profit Business and Human Rights Resource Center (BHRRC), to The Diplomat.

The BHRRC and other watchdogs like Human Rights Watch, Somo, The Breakthrough Institute, and Walk Free, have found that most companies aren’t meeting their commitments. Across the Global South, especially in Asia, where most goods are manufactured, labor rights continue to be violated by those supplying global brands.

But things are changing. There’s a growing call for mandatory regulations in key importing markets like the United States, Canada, and Europe. This year, new forced labor laws are being passed in places like Vietnam and India, partly due to tariff threats from the United States. While still not universal, they are signs we may be heading to a new paradigm where supply chains are monitored not by nonprofits and the media, but but strict laws and real financial repercussions.

While this will most directly impact countries like China, where state-mandated forced labor of Uyghurs has been well-documented, the entire Asia-Pacific region needs to pay attention or face similar restrictions on foreign market access.

There are numerous reasons why voluntary efforts have mostly failed to have the impact that was once hoped for. To Blankenbach, a key issue is accountability.

“In the voluntary system, there is no central or reliable oversight. Some was done by NGOs, but due to limited resources, that was not comprehensive, and there was no way to sanction companies that weren’t complying,” said Blankenbach.

In general, organizations like CGF or the U.N. rarely monitored members of their voluntary groupings. It was often non-profits like the BHRRC, or the media, that exposed the failures of companies to meet their commitments. And even then, the punishment was often little more than public shaming.

“For things like the Global Compact, strongest enforcement would be, maybe, an exclusion of a member,” said Blankenbach.

Another issue is that competitors aren’t always held to the same standards, especially if they’re based outside the United States, Europe, or a few other markets where consumers demand sustainability, like Japan. An American shoe company could invest heavily into making its supply chains ethical, only to see a Chinese or Vietnamese competitor undercut it on costs, and face far less pressure.

There is also the cost issue. It can be expensive to properly manage one’s supply chain, and that can put a company at a disadvantage. In a world where investors are focused on quarterly returns, that can be challenging.

“Under current market conditions, it may be a short-term economic or financial disadvantage to invest in due diligence,” said Blankenbach.

By contrast, mandatory human rights due diligence law would put legal requirements on companies to ensure that forced labor, coercion, social abuses, and more, don’t exist at all within a supply chain. And if violations are found, a company can face legal or financial repercussions. It’s a market shift from the voluntary model, and puts governments in the center of enforcement.

The benefit of a mandatory law is that it can even the playing field, putting the same requirement on all companies, or at least all companies of a similar size. In fact, some companies support mandatory due diligence for this very reasons.

The best example of a strong due diligence law is the United States’ 2022 Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA). It was focused on one region – Xinjiang in China, the homeland of the Uyghur people. Since at least 2018, Uyghurs have been subjected to various crimes against humanity, including the largest system of concentration camps since World War II, housing at its height perhaps as many as 3 million Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslim minorities. Alongside this is ongoing cultural genocide, as mosques, cemeteries, shrines, and historic Uyghur neighborhoods have all been destroyed.

“The Uyghur people are facing a humanitarian crisis, and countries around the world must treat it with the urgency it deserves,” Elfidar Iltebir, a Uyghur American and president of the Uyghur American Association, told The Diplomat.

But, for businesses, the big news was the increasingly irrefutable evidence that mass-scale, state-sanctioned forced labor of Uyghurs is being used in farms and factories throughout the region. Goods made with Uyghurs’ forced labor are flowing into global supply chains, with cotton, tomatoes and solar panels just a few of the sectors implicated.

There are two things that made what is happening in Xinjiang unique when

analysis.tldr: New strict legal rules on factory working conditions across Asia mean Indian factories will face higher compliance costs, which could impact profit margins for export-focused companies.
the_story: For over 20 years, initiatives like the United Nations Global Compact relied on voluntary guidelines for companies to respect labor and human rights, but watchdogs found most companies failed to meet them.
Experts point out that voluntary systems lacked real oversight, financial penalties, or accountability beyond public shaming or exclusion from groups.

Importing markets like the United States, Canada, and Europe are now shifting toward mandatory human rights laws, with India and Vietnam even passing new forced labor laws partly due to US tariff threats.

The United States passed the 2022 Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) targeting state-sanctioned forced labor in China's Xinjiang region, impacting global supply chains for cotton, tomatoes, and solar panels.
analysis.what_happened: Global brands and importing countries are moving away from voluntary ethical guidelines because companies failed to fix labor abuses on their own. Governments are now introducing strict mandatory laws and real financial punishments, pushing manufacturing hubs like India to adopt new labor regulations to protect their exports.
analysis.analogy: It is like moving from an honor system where shops promised to keep food clean to having health inspectors hand out heavy fines if they find any violations.
why_it_matters_india: India passes new forced labor laws to avoid tariff threats and penalties from major importing countries like the United States.
Indian factories that export goods to Western markets must spend more money auditing and managing their supply chains to prove no labor abuses occurred.
Higher operational costs squeeze profit margins for Indian manufacturing and export companies.
Complying with these laws levels the playing field against competitors who previously cut corners on worker rights.

impacts.rationale: Stricter mandatory checks and potential penalties raise compliance costs, which can temporarily hurt profits for companies selling abroad — generally bad for stock investors in those sectors.

Implementation details of India's newly passed forced labor regulations

history.title: The embargo that rewired the world economy
history.what: Arab oil producers cut output and embargoed several countries during the Yom Kippur war. Oil went from about $3 a barrel to $12 within months, and the industrial world discovered how completely it depended on a resource it did not control.
history.why: Oil demand had grown for two decades on the assumption of permanently cheap supply, so there was no spare capacity and no stockpile anywhere. The producers realised they had collective pricing power and used it. A political event became an economic one because no buffer existed.
history.impact: Stagflation — high inflation and high unemployment together, which economists had thought nearly impossible. US shares fell about 48%. Petrol rationing across the West. For oil-importing India, the import bill and inflation both surged.
history.policy: Strategic petroleum reserves were created so a political shock could not immediately become a price shock. Fuel-efficiency standards were imposed on cars. Nuclear and, much later, renewable programmes were accelerated. The International Energy Agency was founded to coordinate responses.
history.consequence: Rich-world oil consumption per unit of output has more than halved since. The reserves and efficiency rules genuinely worked, which is why later oil shocks — including 2022 — hurt considerably less than 1973 did.
history.pattern: A concentrated supply of something essential is a standing political risk, whatever the price chart says. The response is always the same — build a buffer, use less, find alternatives — and it takes about a decade to work.
history.india_echo: India imports over 85% of its crude, so this is the permanent structural weakness behind the rupee, inflation and the current account deficit. It is also why India's solar push and its own strategic reserve are macro stories, not environmental ones.
history.watch_for: Any critical input where a handful of countries control most of the supply. Rare earths, advanced chips and lithium are today's version of the question.
